entities.name: Newel K. Whitney
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Newel Kimball Whitney (died September 23, 1850) emerged as a central figure in the nascent Latter Day Saint movement during its formative years in the American Midwest, particularly in Kirtland, Ohio, and later Nauvoo, Illinois. A successful Kirtland merchant and entrepreneur, Whitney's early conversion and subsequent financial acumen provided critical infrastructure and monetary support for the fledgling Church of Christ (later The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints). His home served as an early gathering place for church leaders, including Joseph Smith, and his business provided essential economic stability during periods of intense communal growth and financial experimentation, such as the Kirtland Safety Society. He was instrumental in managing the church's temporal affairs, influencing its economic development and community building efforts across the American frontier.

Born in Marlborough, Vermont, Whitney established a thriving general store and ashery in Kirtland, Ohio, by the 1820s, becoming a prominent local businessman. Initially a follower of the Disciples of Christ (Campbellites), he, along with his wife Elizabeth Ann Smith, converted to the Church of Christ in late 1830, influenced by the preaching of Parley P. Pratt and Oliver Cowdery, and the earlier conversion of his Campbellite bishop, Sidney Rigdon. Joseph Smith and his family resided with the Whitneys in Kirtland from 1831 to 1832, during which time several key revelations, including those pertaining to the organization of the church's financial stewardship, were received. Whitney served as the second bishop of the church, presiding over the Kirtland stake from 1831 to 1838, and later as a bishop in Nauvoo, administering both ecclesiastical and temporal affairs, including the intricate financial dealings of the church's mercantile and banking ventures.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Newel K. Whitney played a pivotal role in the early financial and administrative development of the Latter Day Saint movement, providing crucial economic stability and leadership during its formative decades. His contributions directly impacted the church's ability to establish communities and sustain its growing membership across the American frontier.
